claims: Surface recombination of plasma radicals is generally considered to limit film conformality during plasma-assisted ALD.
Film penetration into high-aspect-ratio structures can give direct information on the recombination probability r of plasma radicals on the growth surface.
A strong material dependence has been observed for recombination of oxygen (O) atoms on SiO2, TiO2, Al2O3, and HfO2.
Using extended plasma exposures, films of SiO2 and TiO2 penetrated extremely deep up to an aspect ratio (AR) of ∼ 900.
Growth of Al2O3 and HfO2 was conformal up to depths corresponding to ARs of ∼ 80 and ∼ 40, respectively.

Quantitative insight into surface recombination is essential for modeling radical-surface interaction and understanding for which materials and conditions conformal film growth is feasible by plasma-assisted ALD.
Plasma-assisted ALD has extended the capabilities of ALD, for instance, in terms of low-temperature processing and the number of materials deposited by ALD.
The usage of SiO2 in self-aligned multiple patterning has led to the breakthrough of plasma ALD in high-volume manufacturing.
Plasma ALD enables the growth of SiO2 at low temperature while providing the required high level of film conformality for self-aligned multiple patterning.
Conformal film growth by plasma ALD is typically challenging due to the loss of reactive plasma radicals through surface recombination.
The surface recombination probability r has a strong impact on the dose of plasma radicals needed to reach film saturation on high-aspect-ratio structures.
Surface recombination often limits the aspect ratio (AR) up to which conformal film growth is practically achievable.
Quantitative information on r is barely reported in the literature and is typically only obtained by complex and indirect measurement techniques.
The AR up to which film growth is achieved can be directly related to the value of r under typical process conditions.
The film penetration depth decreases with r and increases with t.
A steady-state exponential decrease in radical density is developed where the flux of incoming radicals is balanced by the recombination loss to the sidewalls.
In the 'recombination-limited' growth regime, an exponential increase in t is required to linearly increase the film penetration depth.
The value of s0 can affect the shape of the coverage profile but typically has a negligible effect on the penetration of radicals into a high-AR structure during film growth.
Film penetration was limited by the plasma half-cycle.
The relatively low conformality of Al2O3 and HfO2 compared with SiO2 and TiO2 is in line with results reported in the literature.
For SiO2 and TiO2, the surface recombination probability appears to be low enough to meet conformality requirements in very demanding applications.
The Al2O3 and HfO2 processes should be able to provide conformal film growth on structures with AR values of 10 to 30 within acceptable cycle times.
For the SiO2 and TiO2 processes, very similar values of r = (6 ± 2) × 10 -5 and (7 ± 4) × 10 -5 are determined.
For TiO2 and HfO2 no literature values have been found (for r).
The values reported for O atom recombination on SiO2 or SiO2-based surfaces show a large spread.
Several experimental factors such as temperature and pressure can cause this spread (in r values).
The surface treatment and roughness can play an important role (in r values).
The properties of the saturated surface during plasma exposure could depend on the precursor used, which may also influence the recombination probability.
An important open question that has received limited attention in the literature is the fundamental reason behind the material dependence of r.
From an atomistic modeling perspective, key factors that play a role are, for instance, the amount of recombination sites and the activation energies for recombination and surface diffusion.
r could be related to measurable material properties such as surface acidity.
